title: Awaken the Giant Within
sources: https://archive.org/download/awaken-the-giant-within-anthony-robbins1/awaken-the-giant-within-anthony-robbins1_djvu.txt (full English text, an annotated study edition, read locally)
source_note: Book text read. DB title 'Icsel Guc' is taken to be Awaken the Giant Within (1991); the text itself names 'Inner Strength' only as an earlier work. The firewalk physics and the 'six human needs' of the old texts do not appear in this book.

facts.claim: Robbins: a belief is 'a feeling of certainty about something'. An idea is like a tabletop with no legs; it will not stand by itself. The legs are references, experiences that back the idea up. 'Those are the legs that make your tabletop solid.'

Sources of references: personal experience, information from other people, books, tapes, movies, and imagination alone. The strongest legs come from personal experiences with a lot of emotion attached, painful or pleasurable; the more references, the stronger the belief. References can be real or imaginary, accurate or inaccurate.
For thousands of years people held the belief that a human could not run a mile in under four minutes. In 1954 Roger Bannister broke that barrier.

Robbins says Bannister got there not merely by physical practice but by constantly rehearsing the event in his mind, breaking the four-minute barrier so many times with such emotional intensity that he created vivid references that became an unquestioned command to his nervous system. (Robbins's account of Bannister's method.)

Robbins writes that the greatest effect of the breakthrough was on others: within one year of Bannister's run 37 other runners broke four minutes, and the year after that 300 did the same. (Figures as given by Robbins; not independently checked.)
Robbins: many people live by 'being realistic' because they failed before; he says most people who keep saying 'let's be realistic' are living in fear of being disappointed again.

Robbins defines a state as the sum of millions of neurological processes, the sum total of our experience at any moment. Forgetting a friend's name or how to spell 'house' is not stupidity, he says, but being in a 'stupid state'. The difference between acting badly or brilliantly is the state of mind and body, not ability.
'To change your ability, change your state.' Two primary ways to change an emotional state: change how you use your body (physiology), or change your focus.

TV analogy: physiology is the electricity the set needs; focus is the channel. 'Emotion is created by motion.' Every emotion has a physiology linked to it: posture, breathing, patterns of movement, facial expressions.

Exercise: swing your arms slowly and routinely like a bored, humorless symphony conductor with a bored face, notice the feeling; then clap your hands explosively and snap them out with a big silly grin and a loud sound, and the feeling changes.
Robbins says people in his Date With Destiny seminar write all the emotions they feel in an average week, and the average is less than a dozen (his claim); we have over eighty muscles in the face.

Robbins worked with John Denver, who had writer's block. They found his best songs had come after something physical: skiing down a mountain, flying his jet or biplane, driving his sports car fast. Frustrations had kept him from the same intense outdoor activity. Robbins says that getting back into a strong physiology restored the flow of his creativity immediately.
